answers.1: Some larger businesses pay Georgia Power hourly 'real-time' prices, and more of them do now. The Public Service Commission (PSC) is deciding how much of that money counts toward 'fuel costs' (the page calls this the 'fuel credit'). The plans also argue over who pays some pipeline fees and whether other costs, like coal rail car leases, get counted. I only saw why it matters once I read that a bigger fuel credit lowers the fuel charge for homes on standard rates, but then that money stops helping pay the rest of the bill. Who decides: the PSC's five commissioners (Jason Shaw, Lauren 'Bubba' McDonald, Peter Hubbard, Alicia M. Johnson and Stan Wise), at a vote set for Dec 15, 2026, 9:30 a.m. The page says they're elected but not when or by whom, so I don't know if I get to vote for them, and it never says what the PSC is or what it normally does. The Options tab threw me by saying 'What lawmakers could have done,' as if lawmakers were involved and it was already over.
answers.2: Lower on one part of my bill, maybe higher on another part later, and the page can't give me a total. If the PSC picks any of the plans the page could read, the fuel credit goes up, which lowers the fuel charge for 'homes and businesses on standard rates' (I assume that's me, but it never says what standard rates are). The same dollars would stop helping pay base costs, and the parties disagree on whether base rates would rise later; 'the next base rate case decides,' and no date is given for that. The only number: Georgia Power estimates each $100 million cuts a typical home's fuel charge by about $1.48 a month, and adds about $1.65 if base rates rise by that much. My own math from those two numbers, not the page's: if both happen, I'd pay about 17 cents a month more for each $100 million. But it never says how many $100 millions any plan moves: Georgia Power's estimates are 'blacked out,' and PIA Staff's are called 'public' but aren't shown. When: it doesn't say when a change would reach my bill. The vote is set for Dec 15, 2026, and the case must be finished by Dec 31, 2026. Why it can't say: the size of the change isn't shown, one side's numbers are hidden, and the base-rate part waits on a later case.
answers.3: It's the money larger businesses pay Georgia Power on hourly real-time prices. Today part of it counts toward fuel costs and, from what I can tell, the rest helps pay base costs (the rest of the bill). A bigger fuel credit moves more of those same dollars to the fuel side: homes and businesses on standard rates get a lower fuel charge, and less of the money helps with base costs, which might mean higher base rates later. The page calls it 'the same dollars,' so it sounds like the money moves from one part of other customers' bills to another part. The plans also fight over pipeline fees: Georgia Power and GIPL want new pipeline fees tied to 'large-load customers' charged to those customers; PIA Staff wants all pipeline and gas storage fees shared by all customers based on monthly energy use; GAM wants no real-time money counted against pipeline fees at all. The page doesn't say whether the businesses end up paying more or less, whether Georgia Power gains or loses anything, or which pipeline plan costs a home like mine less.
answers.4: 1) Send a public comment to the PSC by 9:30 a.m. on Dec 14, 2026 (24 hours before the Dec 15 vote; if the vote moves, the deadline moves). The PSC's comment page doesn't say how to send one, so I'd call the PSC at 404-656-4501 (1-800-282-5813 from outside metro Atlanta) and press 2, or email gapsc@psc.state.ga.us, to ask. 2) Maybe speak at the hearing on Nov 12, 2026 (listed at 9:35 a.m.; arrive about 30 minutes early to sign in), but the page says no filing says whether the public will be heard that day, so I'd call first. It also doesn't say where that hearing is. If I'd rather not speak, I can ask during the hearing to have written comments put in the record. 3) Watch the Dec 15 vote at 9:30 a.m. in hearing room 110, 244 Washington St., Atlanta; it's open to the public. 4) Read the case files on the PSC's web page for Docket 57171. If I needed disability help, I'm told to call the PSC's Executive Secretary's Office at least a day ahead, but no number is given for it. What it doesn't tell me: which plan would lower my bill the most, so I wouldn't know what to ask for in a comment.
answers.5: The page doesn't explain them on this screen. Each argument card shows 'Evidence, by part:' and then labels like 'Supported' and 'Mixed' (one card shows 'Supported' and 'Uncertain'). It says one rule sets every label and points to a 'How to read these cards' link I'd have to tap. Going only by the everyday words, and this is my guess, not the page: 'Mixed' sounds like some evidence for and some against, and 'Uncertain' sounds like nobody knows yet. I also can't tell which 'part' of an argument each label goes with, because the parts aren't named.
answers.6: For a change: PIA Staff and GIPL say fuel-related costs now left out of the credit, such as coal rail car leases, fall on customers who pay the fuel charge, so more of them should count. Against: GAM (manufacturers that use a lot of power) says a bigger fuel credit 'would put upward pressure on base rates,' because that real-time money now lowers other customers' base costs. I didn't see any card arguing to keep today's method as a whole; GAM's 'limit the shift' card is the closest.

seemed_to_favor: Mostly even. Every argument card names who disagrees, it says the named voices are the parties' witnesses and not a head count, and it never brings up political parties. A few things nudged me, though. (1) Saying Georgia Power's estimates are 'blacked out,' with no reason given, made Georgia Power look like it was hiding something next to PIA Staff's 'public' numbers. (2) The background (May 28) gives only one reason for the review, making sure big customers 'pay their share,' plus a worry that today's method raised other customers' fuel costs, so I leaned toward a change before reading any arguments. (3) GAM is described as big power users, so its argument read as self-interest, while GIPL is only 'interfaith' with 'member congregations,' which sounded like the good guys; the page never says who GIPL speaks for or what its stake is. (4) The Option 1 card gives no reason why Georgia Power and GIPL want it, while the Option 2 card gives PIA Staff's reason. (5) No card argues for keeping today's method as a whole, and Resource Supply Management's view is left out entirely. I couldn't judge the evidence labels because they aren't explained here, but GIPL's pipeline card is the only one with no 'Supported' and GAM's 'limit the shift' card is the only 'Uncertain,' so those two looked weakest.
hardest: Question 2. The page gives a per-$100 million example but never says how many $100 millions any plan moves, and the fuel cut ($1.48) and the possible base increase ($1.65) point opposite ways, with the base part left to a later case that has no date, so I couldn't tell if I'd come out ahead or behind.
